title: Section 139 — Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging

content.overview: BNS s. 139 — Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging. Historical concordance: IPC 363A. For conduct governed by the BNS, cite BNS section 139; the IPC reference is historical concordance.
In student language: BNS s. 139 is the rule on “Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging”. The section provides that (1) Whoever kidnaps any child or, not being the lawful guardian of such child, obtains the custody of the child, in order that such child may be employed or used for the purposes of begging shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 139 exists so that “Kidnapping or maiming a child for purposes of begging” has a closed legal test in Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: Homicide, organised crime, terrorism, hurt, acid, restraint, assault, kidnapping and trafficking.

The provision in detail
139. (1) Whoever kidnaps any child or, not being the lawful guardian of such child, obtains the custody of the child, in order that such child may be employed or used for the purposes of begging shall be punishable with rigorous imprisonment for a term which shall not be less than ten years but which may extend to imprisonment for life, and shall also be liable to fine

(2) Whoever maims any child in order that such child may be employed or used for the purposes of begging shall be punishable with imprisonment which shall not be less than twenty years, but which may extend to life which shall mean imprisonment for the remainder of that person’s natural life, and with fine

(3) Where any person, not being the lawful guardian of a child employs or uses such child for the purposes of begging, it shall be presumed, unless the contrary is proved, that he kidnapped or otherwise obtained the custody of such child in order that such child might be employed or used for the purposes of begging

(4) In this section “begging” means—

(i) soliciting or receiving alms in a public place, whether under the pretence of singing, dancing, fortune telling, performing tricks or selling articles or otherwise;

(ii) entering on any private premises for the purpose of soliciting or receiving alms;

(iii) exposing or exhibiting, with the object of obtaining or extorting alms, any sore, wound, injury, deformity or disease, whether of himself or of any other person or of an animal;

(iv) using such child as an exhibit for the purpose of soliciting or receiving alms

Definitions and key terms
“begging” — — (i) soliciting or receiving alms in a public place, whether under the pretence of singing, dancing, fortune telling, performing tricks or selling articles or otherwise.

learningObjectives: Master the severe statutory regime suppressing child begging syndicates under BNS s. 139.
Analyze sub-section (1) penalizing kidnapping or obtaining custody of a child for begging: mandatory minimum seven years up to ten years, and fine.
Examine sub-section (2) penalizing the maiming of a child for begging: mandatory imprisonment for life (not less than ten years) and fine.
Understand the broad statutory definition of 'begging' and evidentiary presumptions under sub-sections (3) and (4).
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 139 establishes severe penalties against child begging syndicates: sub-section (1) punishes whoever kidnaps any child or, not being the lawful guardian, obtains custody of a child in order that such child may be employed or used for begging with imprisonment of not less than seven years but which may extend to ten years, and fine; sub-section (2) punishes whoever maims any child in order that such child may be employed or used for begging with imprisonment for life, which shall not be less than ten years, and fine.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Suppresses organized begging cartels by imposing severe mandatory minimum sentences of seven to ten years for child begging and life imprisonment for the barbaric maiming of children.
statutoryFramework: Chapter VI — Of Offences Affecting the Human Body, BNS s. 139 (corresponding to IPC s. 363A).
Sub-section (1): Kidnapping or obtaining custody of child for begging — imprisonment not less than seven years extending to ten years, and fine.
Sub-section (2): Maiming any child for begging — imprisonment for life (not less than ten years), and fine.
Sub-section (3): Presumption of intent to beg when a non-guardian kidnaps/obtains custody and child is found begging.
Sub-section (4): Presumption of maiming for begging when a child in custody is found maimed.
Definition: Comprehensive definition of 'begging' covering soliciting alms in public under pretence of singing, dancing, or exposing sores.
essentialIngredients: For sub-section (1): The victim is a child (under eighteen years).
The accused kidnapped the child, or obtained custody without being the lawful guardian.
The act was done in order that the child be used or employed for begging.
For sub-section (2): The accused maimed the child (inflicted permanent bodily mutilation or deformity).
The maiming was done in order that the child be employed or used for begging.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 139 targets the horrific reality of organized begging syndicates that kidnap children or buy them from impoverished families to exploit them as street beggars. Sub-section (1) penalizes anyone who kidnaps a child or obtains custody (not being the legal guardian) to use the child for begging, mandating a severe sentence of seven to ten years imprisonment. Sub-section (2) targets the monstrous practice of intentionally maiming children—amputating limbs, gouging eyes, or burning flesh to evoke public sympathy and maximize alms—punishing offenders with mandatory imprisonment for life (which cannot be less than ten years) and fine. Sub-sections (3) and (4) provide decisive statutory presumptions: if a person has custody of a child who is found begging or maimed, the court presumes the unlawful intent until the contrary is proved.
examples: Teaching example (Sub-section 1 - Kidnapping for begging): An operative of a street syndicate kidnaps a five-year-old child from a railway station and forces the child to beg at traffic intersections. Under s. 139(1), the operative faces seven to ten years imprisonment.

Teaching example (Sub-section 2 - Maiming child): Gang leaders intentionally amputate a kidnapped seven-year-old child's hand with a cleaver and pour acid on the wound to create a permanent stump for street begging. The offenders are liable under s. 139(2) to mandatory life imprisonment (minimum 10 years).
distinctions: Section 139(1) vs Simple Kidnapping (s. 137): Simple kidnapping carries up to 7 years; Section 139(1) imposes a mandatory minimum of 7 years extending to 10 years when done for begging.
Section 139(2) vs Grievous Hurt (s. 117): Grievous hurt carries up to 7 years; Section 139(2) mandates imprisonment for life (minimum 10 years) for maiming a child for begging.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a non-relative caught housing three maimed minor children who were sent out daily to beg at city temples is liable under s. 139.
Rule: Having custody of a child who is maimed and found begging triggers statutory presumptions under BNS s. 139(3) and (4).
Application: The accused is not a lawful guardian, the children were maimed, and they were used for begging.
Conclusion: The accused is liable under BNS s. 139(1) and (2) facing life imprisonment.

keyTakeaways: Severe penal statute targeting child begging cartels.
Sub-section (1): Kidnapping/custody for begging (mandatory 7 to 10 years and fine).
Sub-section (2): Maiming a child for begging (mandatory life imprisonment, not less than 10 years).
Sub-sections (3) and (4) establish powerful statutory presumptions against custodians.
